title: Newborn Transition: Recognize Failure to Adapt Early
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Most newborns transition without advanced intervention, but persistent central cyanosis, apnea/gasping, marked work of breathing, poor tone, bradycardia, or failure to improve requires immediate escalation and neonatal-resuscitation support according to current protocol.
recognize: Transient acrocyanosis can be expected early; central cyanosis, persistent low oxygenation, grunting/retractions or apnea are not normal adaptation.
Temperature, glucose, gestational age, infection risk and perinatal events can destabilize transition.
priorities: Support warmth, airway positioning and drying/stimulation per current neonatal-resuscitation practice while rapidly identifying whether ventilation support is needed.
Escalate persistent apnea/gasping, severe respiratory distress, bradycardia, poor perfusion or neurologic depression.
assessMonitor: Trend respirations/work of breathing, heart rate, tone, color/perfusion, oxygenation when indicated, temperature and feeding readiness.
interventions: Maintain thermoregulation, skin-to-skin when appropriate, and protocol-based neonatal support; avoid delaying rescue for routine weighing/bathing/documentation.
medicationSafety: Resuscitation medications are protocol-driven and uncommon compared with effective ventilation; PN/LVN role depends on neonatal setting competency and policy.
teaching: Explain that skin color of hands/feet can differ from central cyanosis and that feeding readiness depends on stable breathing and temperature.
delegationScope: Neonatal resuscitation roles require trained team members and facility policy; unstable newborn assessment/escalation remains licensed clinical responsibility.
examTrap: Continuing stimulation while a newborn who is apneic or gasping needs effective ventilation support.
oneLinePearl: In neonatal transition, breathing and heart rate decide urgency.

title: Newborn Thermoregulation: Prevent Cold Stress Before It Cascades
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Newborns lose heat rapidly. Hypothermia increases oxygen and glucose consumption and can worsen respiratory distress and hypoglycemia, especially in preterm or low-birth-weight infants.
recognize: Low temperature, cool skin, lethargy, poor feeding, tachypnea, hypoglycemia or increased oxygen need can accompany cold stress.
Evaporation, convection, conduction and radiation all contribute to neonatal heat loss.
priorities: Dry/warm promptly after birth, use skin-to-skin or regulated thermal support as appropriate, and recheck temperature after interventions.
Escalate persistent hypothermia, respiratory deterioration, lethargy or hypoglycemia.
assessMonitor: Trend axillary/core temperature per policy, respiratory status, glucose risk, feeding and environmental heat-loss sources.
interventions: Use warm blankets, hat, skin-to-skin, warmed environment/incubator as ordered; delay bathing until thermal stability is established.
medicationSafety: Medication dosing and oxygen needs may be affected indirectly by physiologic instability; correct thermal stress rather than treating downstream abnormalities in isolation.
teaching: Keep the newborn warm but avoid overheating; use one additional light layer compared with an adult when appropriate and follow safe-sleep guidance.
delegationScope: Routine temperature measurement can be delegated with thresholds; persistent instability requires licensed reassessment.
examTrap: Bathing a newly born infant before temperature stability is established.
oneLinePearl: A cold newborn burns glucose and oxygen to get warm.

title: Newborn Hypoglycemia: Feed Early, Escalate Symptoms Fast
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
bottomLine: Risk-based glucose screening is most important in infants with maternal diabetes, prematurity, growth restriction, large size or clinical symptoms. Symptomatic hypoglycemia is urgent because neurologic injury risk increases with severe or persistent low glucose.
recognize: Jitteriness, lethargy, poor feeding, apnea, cyanosis, temperature instability or seizure can signal hypoglycemia but are nonspecific.
A well-appearing at-risk infant still requires the unit's screening/feeding protocol.
priorities: Support early effective feeding when appropriate and obtain glucose per protocol.
Escalate symptomatic, very low, recurrent or treatment-resistant hypoglycemia promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose values, feeding effectiveness, temperature, respiratory status, neurologic behavior and maternal/gestational risk factors.
interventions: Implement protocol-based feeding, dextrose gel or IV dextrose only as ordered/authorized; recheck response on schedule.
medicationSafety: Concentrated dextrose and IV therapy require neonatal dosing/line safeguards; PN/LVN authority varies by setting.
teaching: Frequent feeding and follow-up screening may be needed even when the infant looks well.
delegationScope: Point-of-care glucose collection may be delegated according to policy; interpretation/treatment escalation remains licensed responsibility.
examTrap: Assuming jitteriness is normal newborn behavior without checking glucose in an at-risk infant.
oneLinePearl: In a symptomatic newborn, check glucose early and treat delay as risk.

title: Newborn Jaundice: Measure Risk, Do Not Judge by Color Alone
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Visible jaundice requires age-in-hours and bilirubin-context assessment. Early, rapidly rising or severe hyperbilirubinemia can progress to acute bilirubin encephalopathy and kernicterus.
recognize: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is particularly concerning and requires prompt evaluation.
Poor feeding, dehydration, prematurity, hemolysis and certain family/clinical histories increase risk.
priorities: Use transcutaneous/serum bilirubin assessment and current treatment thresholds rather than visual inspection alone.
Escalate very early jaundice, lethargy, poor suck, abnormal tone, high-pitched cry or concerning bilirubin trajectory.
assessMonitor: Trend bilirubin values by age, feeding/output, weight loss, hydration, neurologic behavior and risk factors.
interventions: Support effective feeding, ordered phototherapy and follow-up timing based on bilirubin risk; protect eyes/skin and temperature as appropriate during phototherapy.
medicationSafety: Do not substitute sunlight exposure for prescribed phototherapy or delay bilirubin measurement because jaundice appears mild.
teaching: Parents should know the follow-up bilirubin/feeding plan and when increasing sleepiness or poor feeding requires urgent reassessment.
delegationScope: Routine observation can be delegated; bilirubin-risk interpretation and treatment escalation require licensed/provider follow-up.
examTrap: Calling visible jaundice physiologic without considering the infant's age in hours.
oneLinePearl: Jaundice is a number-and-timing problem, not a color judgment.
sourceBasis: AAP 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Management of Hyperbilirubinemia in the Newborn Infant 35 or More Weeks of Gestation, current through 2026

title: Newborn Feeding Safety: Coordinate Suck, Swallow, Breathe
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Safe newborn feeding requires physiologic stability and coordinated suck-swallow-breathe. Recurrent coughing, cyanosis, bradycardia, apnea, fatigue or poor transfer is not solved by pushing the feeding harder.
recognize: Feeding difficulty may reflect prematurity, respiratory illness, neurologic dysfunction, anatomic problems, sepsis, hypoglycemia or jaundice.
Effective feeding is assessed by latch/suck, transfer, output, weight trend and infant tolerance—not minutes at the breast/bottle alone.
priorities: Pause feeding with distress, position safely, and escalate recurrent choking, cyanosis, apnea or poor endurance.
Assess feeding technique, respiratory stability and hydration/weight trend.
assessMonitor: Observe coordination, respiratory rate/effort, color, fatigue, intake/output, weight and caregiver technique.
interventions: Use paced, cue-based feeding and lactation/feeding support as appropriate; avoid force-feeding a distressed infant.
medicationSafety: Medication administration mixed into feeds must account for full-dose delivery and feeding tolerance; do not place medications in a full bottle the infant may not finish.
teaching: Feed on infant cues and stop when the infant shows stress; seek help for persistent poor feeding or fewer expected wet diapers.
delegationScope: Routine feeding may be performed by trained caregivers/staff; recurrent physiologic instability requires licensed assessment.
examTrap: Continuing a bottle because the prescribed volume is not finished despite cyanosis and coughing.
oneLinePearl: A safe feed is coordinated, not forced.

title: Safe Sleep: Back, Flat, Firm, Bare
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Safe sleep places the infant supine on a firm, flat, noninclined surface without pillows, loose blankets, bumpers, positioners or soft objects. Room-sharing without bed-sharing reduces sleep-related risk.
recognize: Prone/side sleep, soft surfaces, inclined sleepers, couches/armchairs, overheating and smoke exposure increase sleep-related risk.
Devices marketed for positioning or routine home cardiorespiratory monitoring do not replace evidence-based safe-sleep practice.
priorities: Model safe sleep every time in hospital and at home teaching.
Correct unsafe positioning/environment immediately and explain why.
assessMonitor: Assess caregiver understanding, sleep environment, smoking/substance exposure and access to a safe sleep surface.
interventions: Use a fitted sheet only on a firm sleep surface; keep soft items out; encourage room-sharing and breastfeeding when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Sedating medications/substances in caregivers can increase unsafe bed-sharing risk and should be addressed in safety planning.
teaching: Back to sleep for every sleep; tummy time is for awake, supervised periods.
delegationScope: All caregivers/staff must follow safe-sleep policy; deviations should be corrected and escalated when medically ordered positioning is not clear.
examTrap: Using side-lying sleep because the parent worries about aspiration in a healthy infant.

title: Umbilical Cord Care: Keep It Clean, Dry, and Watch for Infection
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Routine cord care is generally clean and dry. Spreading erythema, purulent drainage, foul odor with systemic signs, fever/hypothermia or poor feeding can indicate omphalitis and requires urgent evaluation.
recognize: A small amount of dried blood after separation may be benign; progressive redness, swelling, tenderness or purulence is not.
Home remedies/powders can contaminate the stump or delay drying.
priorities: Keep the stump exposed to air and diaper folded below it when practical.
Escalate spreading redness, purulent drainage or any systemic illness signs promptly.
assessMonitor: Inspect stump/skin, temperature, feeding, activity and signs of systemic infection.
interventions: Use clean hands and dry cord care unless local/public-health guidance specifies otherwise.
medicationSafety: Do not apply antiseptics, powders or topical antibiotics routinely without an indication/order.
teaching: Let the cord fall off naturally; do not pull it and seek care for infection signs.
delegationScope: Routine observation can be delegated; suspected omphalitis requires licensed/provider evaluation.
examTrap: Treating foul drainage and spreading redness as normal separation.
oneLinePearl: Dry cord is routine; red, draining, sick newborn is urgent.
sourceBasis: WHO dry cord care principles as applicable in high-resource U.S. settings

title: Circumcision Aftercare: Control Bleeding, Protect Healing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After circumcision, small spotting can be expected, but persistent bleeding, inability to void, progressive swelling, discoloration or infection signs require prompt escalation.
recognize: A yellowish healing film can be normal; purulence with increasing erythema, systemic illness or foul drainage is concerning.
No urine within the expected postprocedure period may indicate swelling/obstruction or another problem.
priorities: Check bleeding and voiding before discharge according to policy.
Escalate active bleeding, increasing swelling, abnormal color/perfusion or failure to void.
assessMonitor: Inspect bleeding, edema/color, urine output, pain/irritability and infection signs.
interventions: Use petroleum or dressing care according to technique/provider instructions; keep diaper area clean and avoid pressure/trauma.
medicationSafety: Use only prescribed/approved neonatal analgesia; avoid aspirin-containing products.
teaching: Demonstrate diaper changes and explain normal healing versus urgent signs.
delegationScope: Postprocedure observation may be within routine PN scope; active bleeding or perfusion concerns require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Calling persistent oozing normal because some spotting is expected.
oneLinePearl: After circumcision, bleeding and urine output are the key discharge checks.

title: Newborn Screening: Hearing, CCHD, Blood Spot—Close the Loop
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Newborn screening is a system, not a single test. Blood-spot screening, hearing screening and pulse-oximetry CCHD screening require correct timing, documentation, follow-up of failed/incomplete screens and communication with the family/provider.
recognize: A failed screen is not the same as a confirmed diagnosis but must not be ignored.
Early discharge, transfusion, prematurity or NICU status can alter timing/repeat-screen requirements.
priorities: Verify required screens are completed or a repeat/follow-up plan is documented before discharge.
Escalate failed CCHD screening or clinically unstable findings immediately.
assessMonitor: Track screen completion/results, gestational/NICU factors, transfusion status when relevant, and follow-up appointments.
interventions: Provide clear family teaching that abnormal screening requires timely confirmatory testing.
medicationSafety: No medication replaces screening; prophylaxis such as vitamin K/erythromycin is separate from state newborn-screening programs.
redFlags: No follow-up plan for failed hearing screen
Incomplete blood-spot screen without repeat plan
teaching: Screening finds risk early; a failed screen means more testing is needed, not that the infant definitely has the condition.
delegationScope: Screen performance may be delegated to trained staff; interpretation, follow-up and escalation require licensed/team responsibility.
examTrap: Reassuring the family that a failed screening test can simply be repeated at the next routine visit without a defined plan.
oneLinePearl: A screening program is only as safe as its follow-up.

title: Preterm Discharge and Car-Seat Safety: Prove Physiologic Readiness
clientNeeds: Health Promotion and Maintenance
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Preterm discharge requires physiologic stability in feeding, temperature, breathing and growth plus safe transportation planning. Infants at risk may need a period of observation in their car seat according to current hospital/AAP policy before discharge.
recognize: Apnea, bradycardia, desaturation or poor positioning can occur in semi-upright devices, especially in smaller/preterm infants.
Car seats are transportation devices, not routine sleep surfaces.
priorities: Verify feeding/temperature/respiratory stability and the discharge follow-up plan.
Ensure caregivers can position/harness the infant correctly and understand that failed observation requires further evaluation/plan.
assessMonitor: Assess growth/feeding, apnea/bradycardia history, oxygen needs, caregiver competence and car-seat fit/position.
interventions: Use rear-facing seat according to manufacturer instructions and hospital policy; minimize time in sitting devices outside travel.
medicationSafety: Home oxygen/monitoring or medications do not make an unstable infant safe for discharge; readiness requires overall physiologic stability.
teaching: Place the seat rear-facing in the back seat and never use the car seat as a routine sleep location outside travel.
delegationScope: Car-seat education/testing requires trained staff per facility policy; discharge-readiness decisions are interdisciplinary.
examTrap: Passing discharge because the infant fits the car seat even though feeding and respiratory stability remain poor.
oneLinePearl: Discharge readiness is physiologic first, equipment second.
